title: Design a Stack With Increment Operation
description:
# Design a Stack With Increment Operation

Design a bounded stack that also supports incrementing a prefix from the bottom of the stack.

Implement the `CustomStack` class:

*   `CustomStack(int maxSize)` initializes the stack with capacity `maxSize`.
*   `void push(int x)` pushes `x` onto the top of the stack if the stack is not full. If the stack is full, the operation does nothing.
*   `int pop()` removes and returns the top element of the stack. If the stack is empty, return `-1`.
*   `void increment(int k, int val)` adds `val` to the bottom `k` elements of the stack. If the stack currently has fewer than `k` elements, increment every current element.

The bottom of the stack is the oldest element that has not been popped. Increment operations must not affect elements that are pushed later after old elements have been popped.

In operation examples, the first array lists operations and the second lists their argument lists, paired by index and executed left to right. The first operation constructs the object; later operations use that same object. Outputs align by index too: constructors and void methods produce `null`; an empty argument list `[]` means no arguments.

## Example 1:

**Input:**
["CustomStack","push","push","pop","push","push","push","increment","increment","pop","pop","pop","pop"]
[[3],[1],[2],[],[2],[3],[4],[5,100],[2,100],[],[],[],[]]
**Output:**
[null,null,null,2,null,null,null,null,null,103,202,201,-1]

**Explanation:**
The extra `push(4)` is ignored because the stack is already full. `increment(5, 100)` increments all three current elements, and `increment(2, 100)` increments only the two bottom elements.

## Example 2:

**Input:**
["CustomStack","push","push","increment","pop","push","pop","pop"]
[[2],[1],[2],[2,10],[],[3],[],[]]
**Output:**
[null,null,null,null,12,null,3,11]

**Explanation:**
After popping `12`, the newly pushed `3` must not inherit the previous increment that was applied to the old top slot.

## Constraints:

*   `1 <= maxSize, x, k <= 1000`
*   `0 <= val <= 100`
*   At most `1000` calls will be made to each method.

tests.description: Overflow push is ignored and increment can cover more than the current size.
Lazy increments accumulate and propagate when upper elements pop first.
A new push after a pop must not inherit increment state from the old top slot.
Incrementing an empty stack has no later effect.
Increment with k = 1 affects only the bottom element.
A size-one stack ignores overflow pushes and can receive multiple increments.

solutions.name: Lazy Increment Array
solutions.description:
## Approach

Store stack values in a fixed array and keep a second `inc` array of pending additions. `increment(k, val)` adds `val` only at the deepest affected index. When that index is popped, its pending value is applied to the popped element and propagated one level lower.

## Key Insight

A bottom-prefix increment affects a contiguous prefix of stack depths. Marking the topmost affected depth is enough because the mark can flow downward exactly when upper elements are removed.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(1) per operation
- Space Complexity: O(n)

solutions.name: Direct Fixed Array Increment
solutions.timeComplexity: O(k) for increment, O(1) for push/pop
solutions.description:
## Approach

Use a fixed array as the stack. Push and pop adjust the top pointer. For `increment`, walk from index zero through the smaller of `k` and the current stack size, adding `val` directly to each stored value.

## Key Insight

This baseline keeps all state explicit. It is slower for large `increment` calls, but it is the easiest version to reason about and a useful correctness reference for optimized approaches.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(k) for increment and O(1) for push/pop
- Space Complexity: O(n)

solutions.name: LinkedList Bottom Iterator
solutions.timeComplexity: O(k) for increment, O(1) for push/pop
solutions.description:
## Approach

Keep the bottom of the stack at the head of a `LinkedList` and the top at the tail. Push appends to the tail, pop removes from the tail, and increment walks from the head with a list iterator to update the bottom `k` nodes.

## Key Insight

A linked representation makes the bottom-to-top order explicit. It trades the classic array layout for a direct traversal of the exact nodes that must be incremented.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(k) for increment and O(1) for push/pop
- Space Complexity: O(n)

solutions.name: Fenwick Range Add Ledger
solutions.timeComplexity: O(log n) per pop/increment, O(1) push
solutions.description:
## Approach

Store raw stack values in an array and use a Fenwick tree as a range-add, point-query ledger over stack depths. `increment` range-adds the bottom affected depths. On pop, query the current top depth and then clear that depth so a later push into the same slot does not inherit old increments.

## Key Insight

The stack depth is an index line. Prefix increments are range additions, and each pop needs only the point value at the current top depth. Clearing the popped point preserves correctness after slots are reused.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(log n) per pop/increment and O(1) push
- Space Complexity: O(n)

solutions.name: Segment Tree Range Add Ledger
solutions.timeComplexity: O(log n) per pop/increment, O(1) push
solutions.description:
## Approach

Store raw stack values in an array and keep a lazy segment tree over stack depths. `increment` applies a range add to `[0, limit - 1]`. `pop` point-queries the current top depth, clears that one depth, and returns the raw value plus the pending increment.

## Key Insight

A segment tree is heavier than the specialized lazy increment array, but it models the operation as a general range update plus point query. It also makes the slot-reuse cleanup explicit.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(log n) per pop/increment and O(1) push
- Space Complexity: O(n)
